stakeholders.name: protestant_reformers
stakeholders.situation: Translate scripture into vernacular languages and distribute via commercial printers, bypassing ecclesiastical gatekeeping. Frame the technology as divine providence making scripture accessible, but actively coordinate printing networks, fund translation projects, and write polemical prefaces. The technology enables but does not determine their organizational strategy.

stakeholders.name: commercial_printers
stakeholders.situation: Profit from vernacular scripture as a high-demand commodity. Print whatever sells; vernacular Bibles and reformist tracts are lucrative because reformers subsidize print runs and reading publics buy them. The technology creates the market opportunity, but printers actively choose vernacular religious material over other genres because reformers pay and readers buy.

stakeholders.name: vernacular_reading_publics
stakeholders.situation: Gain direct access to scripture in languages they read, without mediation by Latin-literate clergy. The technology makes this physically possible, but reformers' translation and distribution work makes it actually available. Their demand sustains the market, but reformers created the supply.

stakeholders.name: latin_ecclesiastical_hierarchy
stakeholders.situation: Lose monopoly control over scriptural interpretation as vernacular texts circulate outside ecclesiastical channels. The hierarchy's authority was constituted through Latin textual control; vernacular dissemination undermines the institutional basis of interpretive authority. They resist through censorship and Index, but the technology's economics favor decentralized production.

stakeholders.name: manuscript_scriptoria
stakeholders.situation: Displaced by mechanized text production. Manuscript copying cannot compete with printing press economics. Their craft becomes economically obsolete as print runs of hundreds replace hand-copied single volumes.

stakeholders.name: secular_authorities
stakeholders.situation: Navigate between ecclesiastical pressure to suppress vernacular scripture and reformist pressure to protect it. Some princes adopt reformation to consolidate territorial authority against Rome; others enforce Catholic censorship. The technology creates the choice, but political calculation determines which side they take.

stakeholders.name: technology_historians
stakeholders.situation: Analyze whether printing technology deterministically caused vernacular scripture spread or whether reformers and printers used available technology to pursue pre-existing theological and commercial goals. The technology made mass dissemination economically feasible, but human agents chose what to print and how to distribute it.

six_questions.coordination_function: Printing technology solves the physical problem of text reproduction at scale: one press can produce hundreds of identical copies where manuscript production required months per copy. This is genuine coordination—standardized texts, reduced copying errors, economies of scale.
six_questions.transfer_function: Moves interpretive authority from Latin-literate ecclesiastical hierarchy to vernacular-reading publics; moves economic value from manuscript scriptoria to commercial printers; moves theological agenda-setting power to reformers who control translation and distribution networks.
six_questions.absent_voices: Illiterate peasants who could not read vernacular texts either, and for whom the shift from Latin to German scripture made no practical difference. They appear in neither reformers' nor hierarchy's accounts because neither side's legitimacy claim depends on their experience.
six_questions.disappearance_rationale: Technology determinists argue the printing press made vernacular scripture inevitable—once the technology existed, economic and information-access pressures would have produced the same outcome regardless of reformers' agency. Reformers and their historians argue the technology was a tool they deployed strategically; without theological motivation and organizational coordination, printers would have printed other material and the hierarchy's Latin monopoly would have persisted longer.
six_questions.founding_problem: Manuscript production was slow, expensive, and error-prone. Reproducing texts at scale required either massive scriptoria (controlled by ecclesiastical institutions) or accepting high error rates as copies diverged from exemplars.
six_questions.founding_problem_corroboration: The founding problem is dead: printing technology solved text reproduction at scale by 1500. Technology historians, economic historians, and both Catholic and Protestant scholars agree the technical problem was solved. The contest is whether solving that problem CAUSED vernacular scripture spread (technology determinism) or merely ENABLED reformers to execute a strategy they would have pursued by other means (human agency). Reformers cite their own organizational records showing deliberate coordination; determinists cite the technology's rapid adoption across all domains, not just religious texts.

commentary.narrative_context: The printing press enabled mass production of vernacular scripture, which reformers used to bypass ecclesiastical gatekeeping of biblical interpretation. The constraint is CLAIMED as mountain (technological determinism: the printing press made vernacular scripture inevitable) while the metrics describe substantial extraction from the Latin hierarchy and active enforcement by reformers coordinating printer networks. This is deliberate FSM authoring: the technology story is the cover; identifiable beneficiaries (reformers, printers) captured the technology's affordances for theological and commercial ends.
commentary.logic_rationale: Extraction rises from 0.15 to 0.68 over the interval as vernacular scripture shifts interpretive authority from hierarchy to reformers and economic value from scriptoria to commercial printers. Suppression rises from 0.25 to 0.72 as reformers actively coordinate distribution networks and the hierarchy deploys censorship (Index Librorum Prohibitorum, 1559) to suppress vernacular texts. Theater rises modestly (0.05 to 0.28) as both sides frame their actions in terms of divine will or textual purity rather than power struggle. Accessibility collapse is moderate (0.62): manuscript production was an alternative, just economically uncompetitive. Resistance is substantial (0.58): the hierarchy fought vernacular dissemination for a century.
commentary.directionality_logic: Protestant reformers and commercial printers are structural beneficiaries: reformers gain theological agenda-setting power, printers gain profitable markets. The Latin ecclesiastical hierarchy is the primary target: loses interpretive monopoly, identity-locked to Latin textual authority. Vernacular reading publics are secondary beneficiaries: gain access, but reformers created the supply. Manuscript scriptoria are secondary targets: economically displaced. The technology made the shift possible, but human agents chose what to print and how to distribute it.
commentary.perspectival_gap: From the reformers' seat, the printing press is divine providence making scripture accessible—a mountain of technological inevitability. From the hierarchy's seat, the same structure is coordinated extraction: reformers weaponized a technology to undermine ecclesiastical authority. From the analytical seat, the technology created affordances that reformers and printers exploited; calling it a mountain erases their agency. The engine computes this divergence from the structural data.
commentary.mandatrophy_analysis: The founding problem (slow, expensive manuscript reproduction) was genuinely solved by printing technology. But the constraint's operation—vernacular scripture dissemination—extracted interpretive authority from the hierarchy and required active coordination by reformers. The technology was necessary but not sufficient; reformers' organizational work and printers' commercial incentives were the sufficient conditions. Calling it pure mountain erases the beneficiaries' agency and the hierarchy's resistance.

omegas.question: Did printing technology deterministically cause vernacular scripture spread, or did reformers and printers use available technology to pursue pre-existing theological and commercial goals?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Comparative analysis of printing adoption across domains: if printers produced vernacular religious texts at higher rates than economic demand alone would predict, reformer subsidy and coordination were causal. If vernacular scripture spread tracks general printing economics, technology was deterministic.
omegas.impact: If technology was deterministic, the constraint is a genuine mountain and reformers were epiphenomenal. If reformers' agency was causal, the constraint is tangled rope or snare—coordination (printing technology) layered with extraction (reformers capturing interpretive authority).
omegas.description: Whether printing technology alone caused vernacular scripture spread or required reformer coordination.

omegas.question: Could the ecclesiastical hierarchy have adopted printing technology to defend Latin textual monopoly, or did the technology's economics structurally favor decentralized vernacular production?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Historical analysis of hierarchy's printing efforts (e.g., Plantin Press, Catholic Counter-Reformation printing) and economic analysis of centralized vs. decentralized printing cost structures.
omegas.impact: If the hierarchy could have used printing to defend its monopoly but failed due to organizational inertia, the technology was neutral and reformers' victory was contingent. If printing economics structurally favored decentralization, the technology was deterministic and the hierarchy's defeat was inevitable.
omegas.description: Whether printing technology's economics structurally favored reformers or was organizationally neutral.

omegas.question: Did vernacular scripture spread benefit illiterate peasants, or did it merely shift textual gatekeeping from Latin-literate clergy to vernacular-literate urban classes?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Literacy rate analysis and ethnographic evidence of how illiterate populations accessed scripture before and after printing (oral transmission, public reading, visual media).
omegas.impact: If illiterate peasants remained excluded, the constraint's beneficiaries are narrower than the reformers' universalist rhetoric claims, and the 'democratization' narrative is a cover story for shifting power between literate classes.
omegas.description: Whether vernacular scripture spread genuinely democratized access or merely shifted gatekeeping.

network.dual_formulation_note: This constraint is one reading of a contested kernel: the relationship between printing technology and religious reformation. A sibling reading would frame the same historical events as pure rope (printing technology as neutral coordination tool) or pure snare (reformers' coordinated extraction from hierarchy with technology as instrument). The ε values differ substantially across readings because the technology-determinism reading attributes low extraction (technology is neutral) while the reformer-agency reading attributes high extraction (reformers captured the technology for theological ends).
